chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Musa ibn Umar, from Salih ibn al-Sindiyy al-Jammal, from a man from the people of Ar-Raqqa who is called Abu Madha', who said:

A man said to me: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'They come to the grave of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and make it their dining mat (sufrah). Indeed, if they came to the graves of their fathers and mothers, they would not do that.' I said: 'So what do they eat?' He said: 'Bread and milk.'

key_terms.الْخُبْزَ وَاللَّبَنَ: Bread and milk, the simple food mentioned as being consumed by visitors at the shrine.
key_terms.سُفْرًا: A large cloth or mat spread on the ground for eating; here used metaphorically for making the grave a place of social gathering and dining.
key_terms.قُبُورَ آبَائِهِمْ وَأُمَّهَاتِهِمْ: The graves of their fathers and mothers, representing ordinary familial burial sites.

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of eating at the grave of Imam al-Husayn according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the unique spiritual magnetism of Imam al-Husayn’s (peace be upon him) shrine, where visitors transform the site into a 'sufrah' (a dining mat) by consuming simple foods like bread and milk, a practice distinct from their customary behavior at ancestral graves. This highlights the concept of *barakah* (blessing) inherent in the Ahl al-Bayt’s resting places, turning the grave into a locus of communal sustenance and spiritual connection rather than merely a place of remembrance.
